performers: Beatrice Harrison, cello; Symphony Orchestra; Edward Elgar, conductor
intro: Beatrice Harrison plays Elgar’s Cello Concerto in E minor, Op. 85, with the composer conducting, barely two months after the concerto’s première. This abridged version of the complete concerto takes up four acoustic record sides and lasts sixteen minutes.

sections.label: A · First side: recitative and E minor theme
sections.mNote: The cello’s opening chords lead into the E minor theme.

sections.label: B · Second side: scherzo
sections.mNote: Plucked chords and fast, lightly bowed notes.

sections.label: C · Third side: Adagio, B♭ major
sections.mNote: A long cello melody in B♭ major.

sections.label: D · Fourth side: the shortened finale
sections.mNote: A resolute cello tune; brisk orchestral replies.

cues.title: Opening cello chords
cues.text: The concerto opens with four chords for solo cello. The orchestra replies quietly, and the soloist follows. The violas then introduce a tune in E minor, which the cello takes over and carries through the movement.
cues.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, p. 1, opening and rehearsals 1–2. The orchestral reply and viola melody are described by Frank Beck: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-a.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nursing home, London, March 1918
cues.text: In March 1918 Elgar had his tonsils removed in a London nursing home. His daughter Carice recalled that he “woke up one morning and asked for pencil and paper and wrote down the opening theme of the Cello Concerto”. This was the 9/8 melody first played by the violas.
cues.evidence: Frank Beck, “Cello Concerto — Creating a Classic”, quoting Carice Elgar Blake; the 9/8 melody as the concerto’s original impetus in Beck’s “A Musical Tour”: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm and https://www.elgar.org/3cello-a.htm

cues.title: First performance, Queen’s Hall, 1919
cues.text: Felix Salmond gave the première on 27 October 1919 at Queen’s Hall, with Elgar conducting the London Symphony Orchestra after too little rehearsal. That December Harrison recorded the new concerto, and the composer conducted again.
cues.evidence: Première and rehearsal circumstances: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm. Harrison’s first session, 22 December 1919: https://archive.org/details/httpsarchive.orgdetailselgar-concerto-for-violoncello-and-orchestra-in-e-minor-op-85-hmv-d-541-545

cues.title: Play-throughs at Brinkwells, June 1919
cues.text: On 2 June 1919, Elgar’s sixty-second birthday, the conductor Landon Ronald visited Brinkwells and heard long passages of the concerto on the piano. Three days later the cellist Felix Salmond tried it on his cello. Alice wrote in her diary: “FS most delighted and enthusiastic.”
cues.evidence: Frank Beck, “Cello Concerto — Creating a Classic”, drawing on Alice Elgar’s diary: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm

cues.title: Score posted to London, 1919
cues.text: On 8 August 1919 Alice took the completed concerto to Fittleworth Post Office and sent it to London. Elgar had spent the summer working at Brinkwells, often rising at four or five in the morning to score it and add new passages.
cues.evidence: Frank Beck’s composition history, drawing on Alice’s diary and the correspondence: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm

cues.title: Scherzo, pizzicato opening and Allegro molto
cues.text: The scherzo opens with pizzicato chords in the cello and repeated trials of a quick figure. In the Allegro molto the solo part plays almost continuous semiquavers, rising and falling.
cues.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, pp. 4–7, rehearsals 18–33: pizzicato recitative, repeated trials of the quick figure and Allegro molto. The second record side is listed as Lento – Allegro molto in the archive description.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: John Barbirolli at the première, 1919
cues.text: Among the London Symphony Orchestra players at the première on 27 October 1919 was a nineteen-year-old cellist, John Barbirolli. In 1965 he conducted the recording with Jacqueline du Pré that many have hailed as the definitive one.
cues.evidence: Frank Beck, “Cello Concerto — Creating a Classic”: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm. Barbirolli in the LSO at the première and the 1965 du Pré recording: Warner Classics, Elgar: Cello Concerto, Sea Pictures, https://www.warnerclassics.com/release/elgar-du-pre

cues.title: Ernest Newman’s review of the première
cues.text: In his review of the première, the critic Ernest Newman complained of a ragged performance. Of the music he wrote: “The work itself is lovely stuff, very simple … a fine spirit’s lifelong wistful brooding upon the loveliness of earth.”
cues.evidence: Ernest Newman’s review of the première, quoted in Frank Beck, “Cello Concerto — Creating a Classic”: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm

cues.title: Letters to Beatrice Harrison, December 1919
cues.text: On 14 December 1919 Elgar sent Beatrice Harrison “the copy with the cuts for the Gramophone”, adding, “I fear it is an awful slaughter but it is the best I can do.” After the session on 22 December he wrote that “recording is rather an ordeal” and thanked her for her “beautiful playing”.
cues.evidence: Elgar to Beatrice Harrison, 14 December 1919 (42 Netherhall Gardens, Hampstead) and Tuesday [23 December 1919] (the Athenaeum): typed transcripts shown in the Museum of Music History exhibition on Beatrice Harrison, https://momh.org.uk/exhibitions/beatrice-harrison-1892-1965/ (image https://momh.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/Image-10.jpg, read). The first session on 22 December 1919 is in the archive item cited in the Salmond note; the second letter’s “yesterday” agrees. Elgar’s preference for Harrison as the concerto’s soloist: Science Museum Group, https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/people/cp169411/beatrice-harrison ; Julian Lloyd Webber, Elgar Society Journal, January 1993, pp. 8–9, https://www.elgarsociety.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/JOURNAL_1993.01.pdf . The earlier note’s claims that she studied the concerto with Elgar and played it at a Royal Philharmonic Society concert in November 1925 rested on Wikipedia alone and are not used.

cues.title: Adagio in B♭ major
cues.text: The cello plays the melody in B♭ major, a key distant from the concerto’s E minor. Elgar marks it molto espressivo. Short rising and falling phrases are linked into a long line, and the orchestra accompanies lightly.
cues.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, p. 8, rehearsals 34–41: Adagio in B♭ major, molto espressivo. Frank Beck discusses its linked phrases: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-a.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Adagio session, Hayes, 1920
cues.text: Harrison and Elgar returned to Hayes on 16 November 1920 to record the slow-movement side used here. The other three sides date from December 1919. HMV issued the two discs in May and June 1921.
cues.evidence: Session dates, the later Adagio matrix HO 4607-AF and release months: https://archive.org/details/httpsarchive.orgdetailselgar-concerto-for-violoncello-and-orchestra-in-e-minor-op-85-hmv-d-541-545

cues.title: Elgar on Schumann, Leipzig, 1883
cues.text: In 1883 Elgar heard Schumann in Leipzig and wrote to a friend: “My ideal!” Thirty-six years later Frank Beck heard Schumannesque echoes in the Adagio. Its B♭ major melody runs from phrase to phrase without a break.
cues.evidence: Frank Beck, “Cello Concerto — A Musical Tour”, on Elgar’s Leipzig visit and the Adagio: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-a.htm

cues.title: Abridged finale, last side
cues.text: The last record side gives the finale four minutes. Its brisk main theme in E minor returns several times in the cello, with firm accents and short orchestral passages between. Harrison and Elgar cut the movement heavily to fit the disc.
cues.evidence: The archive identifies the abridged finale and its four-minute side: https://archive.org/details/httpsarchive.orgdetailselgar-concerto-for-violoncello-and-orchestra-in-e-minor-op-85-hmv-d-541-545. The accented main theme appears in the Novello solo-cello part, p. 9, rehearsal 44.

cues.title: Dedication and letter to Colvin, 1919
cues.text: The dedication names Sidney and Frances Colvin, friends of the Elgars. In late July 1919, when the work was nearly finished, Elgar wrote to Sidney that it was “a real large work and I think good and alive”.
cues.evidence: Elgar to Sidney Colvin, late July 1919; dedication and letter quoted by Frank Beck: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm

cues.title: Last illness, 1933
cues.text: During his last illness, in 1933, Elgar hummed the concerto’s opening theme to a friend. He said that if, after his death, anyone heard someone whistling this tune on the Malvern Hills, there was no cause for alarm: “It’s only me.”
cues.evidence: Frank Beck, “Cello Concerto — Creating a Classic”: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm

transitions.title: Pizzicato join into the second movement
transitions.from: A · First side: recitative and E minor theme
transitions.how: The first movement ends with three plucked cello notes in E minor. The second movement opens with plucked chords, marked Lento, before the cello takes up the bow for a quick semiquaver figure. Elgar wrote attacca in the score; on these records the two movements occupy separate sides.
transitions.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, pp. 3–4, rehearsals 17–18. The archive lists a four-minute first side followed by the second movement: https://archive.org/details/httpsarchive.orgdetailselgar-concerto-for-violoncello-and-orchestra-in-e-minor-op-85-hmv-d-541-545

transitions.title: From the scherzo to the Adagio
transitions.to: C · Third side: Adagio, B♭ major
transitions.how: The scherzo’s running semiquavers end in a few plucked strokes. On the third side, the cello begins the B♭ major Adagio with a rising bowed phrase marked molto espressivo, and the orchestra accompanies the long melody that follows.
transitions.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, pp. 7–8, rehearsals 33–34. The first two recorded sides last 4:00 and 3:52 in the archive’s listing.

transitions.title: From the Adagio to the finale
transitions.from: C · Third side: Adagio, B♭ major
transitions.to: D · Fourth side: the shortened finale
transitions.how: The B♭ major Adagio ends with the cello slowing into a held note. The fourth side goes back to the E minor finale, with accented cello phrases and brisk orchestral replies. The main tune of the finale is marked Allegro ma non troppo, and the solo part is marked risoluto.
transitions.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, pp. 8–9, rehearsals 41 and 44. The archive places the finale after sides lasting 4:00, 3:52 and 3:58; its opening is abridged.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Beatrice Harrison (cello), Symphony Orchestra (orchestra, as on the labels), Edward Elgar (conductor)
fields.note: The archive quotes Moore on the ensemble’s New Symphony/Royal Albert Hall identity; the published credit follows the photographed labels rather than silently expanding their wording.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Four acoustic sides, one movement per side; the whole concerto is abridged.
fields.note: This is the abridged whole concerto, not the complete score or a sixteen-minute finale. The supplied stream already joins all four sides. Only a continuous early finale passage is aligned with the complete Skidmore finale; neither complete work durations nor omitted music are equated. The exact cuts and acoustic-session instrumental substitutions are not established, so no modern-score orchestra timeline is projected onto this recording.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The later session applies to replacement side three, HO 4607-AF. The finale, HO 4198-AF, belongs to the December 1919 session; the listen ID names the two-session recording rather than dating every side to 1920.

The eligibility is based on the issued sound recording, not the composition. No unrestricted modern restoration licence is invented.

composer.epithet: Composer of the Enigma Variations, a set of variations drawn from his friendships, who also recorded his own music for the gramophone.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn as a member of the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. He knew each player in this orchestra individually and had to write within their capabilities. He also taught in local schools and gave private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
